title: Post-normal science

definition.text: A problem-solving approach for science used in policy when 'facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent', developed by Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz in the 1990s.

facts.text: In such cases it sets aside the traditional ideal of truth and focuses on quality, judged by internal and extended peer communities.
Its diagram plots system uncertainties against decision stakes, separating applied science, professional consultancy and post-normal science.
It complements risk analysis and cost-benefit analysis rather than replacing them.
It is meant to guide knowledge for decisions on pandemics, ecosystem collapse, biodiversity loss and sustainability transitions; ecosystem services are a topical subject for it.
In modelling it favours 'models to map our ignorance about the future' over models to predict and control it.
Critics say it adds no new epistemology, turns climate scientists into 'stealth advocates', and undermines empiricism.

contested_note: Critics argue it retraces older debates and weakens scientific neutrality and empiricism.

definition.text: In post-normal science, the wider group of stakeholders, beyond scientists, who share in checking the quality of scientific inputs to a decision.

facts.text: Participants are not treated as passive learners convinced by experts but resolve issues through debate and dialogue.
These spaces express differing values and power in a setting of inequality and conflict, so agreement is not guaranteed.
Some argue conservation science, with its many layers of policy-makers and stakeholders, has always been an extended peer community.

definition.text: Quantitative techniques linked to post-normal science: NUSAP for numbers, sensitivity auditing for indicators and models, quantitative storytelling and MuSIASEM.

facts.text: Post-normal science defines 'garbage in, garbage out' as when input uncertainties must be hidden lest model outputs become completely indeterminate.

definition.text: A worldview that sees Earth as a spaceship with limited supplies, whose passengers must act as one crew for the common good.

facts.text: The earliest known use is in Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879).
Kenneth Boulding's 1966 essay contrasted the past 'cowboy economy' of seemingly endless resources with a future 'spaceman economy' with no unlimited reservoirs for extraction or pollution.
Boulding argued the economic system must fit itself to an ecological system with limited pools of resources.
Buckminster Fuller popularised the phrase in his 1968 Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth.
UN Secretary-General U Thant used it on Earth Day 1971, referring to the services Earth provides and our duty to protect it.
Sociologist Steffen Roth argues a realised Spaceship Earth would be the most total institution in human history.

definition.text: A family of non-equilibrium macroeconomic models built on strict accounting so that every flow and stock in an economy is included and adds up.

facts.text: They are popular in the post-Keynesian school and contrast with the DSGE models of mainstream macroeconomics.
Their accounting rule is that one party's asset is another's liability and no money comes from or vanishes into nowhere.
Wynne Godley used them to warn from 2000 that the US housing market would weaken and cause a recession.
They are now widely used in ecological macroeconomics, adding resource, energy and ecosystem stocks and flows, drawing on Georgescu-Roegen's flow-fund models.
